content: The term labium (plural: labia) originates from Latin and translates to lip. In medical terminology, labium and its derivatives, such as labial and labrum, are used to describe any lip-like structure. However, in English, the term labium is most commonly associated with parts of the vulva. The labia majora are lip-like structures primarily composed of skin and adipose tissue. They extend on either side of the vulva and, following puberty, are typically covered with pubic hair. When a person is standing or has their legs together, the labia majora usually cover, either partially or entirely, the other components of the vulva. The labia minora, also referred to in older terminology as nymphae, are two soft folds of skin located within the labia majora and positioned on either side of the vaginal opening. Anteriorly, the labia minora converge superiorly at the clitoris. The clitoris itself is situated at the anterior aspect of the vulva, and its visible portion, known as the clitoral glans, is partially or entirely covered by a fold of tissue called the clitoral hood. The appearance of the labia, including their coloration, size, and general morphology, varies significantly among individuals. In some women, the labia minora may be nearly absent, while in others, they can be fleshy and protruding. It is not uncommon for the labia minora to be asymmetrical. These variations can be attributed to personal anatomical differences or genetic factors. A notable example of genetic influence is observed in the Khoisan peoples, where the labia minora, often referred to as Khoikhoi aprons, can elongate and extend up to four inches beyond the labia majora when standing. During sexual arousal, the labia become engorged with blood, leading to slight swelling and a change in coloration, typically darkening or reddening. Labiaplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the reshaping or modification of the labia. This procedure is considered controversial within the field of plastic surgery.
